title: Autonomous Data Products for the Autonomous Era: Rethinking Data Architecture for GenAI
gist: Nextdata's VP engineering argues GenAI projects fail on data access operations rather than model quality, and proposes autonomous data products — running processes with their own kernel that encapsulate data, metadata, quality contracts and multiple output modalities (SQL, files, embeddings, MCP) — as the container-and-orchestration layer data is missing. The safety mechanism is policy-as-contract enforced at deploy and runtime like a Kubernetes admission controller, and the context mechanism is progressive tool discovery through a single MCP gateway that exposes only task-relevant tools to avoid context rot.

themes.theme: Why GenAI projects die at data access

insights.claim: The most consistent failure mode in GenAI, deep learning and analytics projects is underestimating the operations and economics around the model rather than choosing a bad model, with data access the single most important piece.
insights.speaker: Jörg Schad
insights.so_what: Reallocates where AI budgets should go — data plumbing and access governance, not model selection, is where projects are won or lost.
insights.quote: The most consistent failure mode I've seen is because we underestimate the economy around it or the operations around it.
insights.locator: Jorg Schad: We're going to be talking about

insights.claim: The recurring enterprise pattern is a consultant-built notebook that demos well on cleaned sample data and breaks when connected to real production data sources and adjacent systems.
insights.speaker: Jörg Schad
insights.so_what: Explains the gap between AI pilot counts and production deployments that shows up in enterprise adoption surveys.
insights.locator: The Bumpy Road from Prototype to Prod

insights.claim: What genuinely changed with GenAI is the speed and scale of data access: consumption shifts from a data scientist who might inspect the data to fleets of autonomous agents querying it continuously.
insights.speaker: Jörg Schad
insights.so_what: Agent-speed consumption removes the human sanity check that previously caught bad or over-exposed data, which is why governance must move into the pipeline.
insights.locator: This is, I think, the only switch to GenAI

insights.claim: The four pillar problems for making enterprise data usable by AI are standardization, speed of access, specificity, and safety.
insights.speaker: Jörg Schad
insights.so_what: A compact evaluation rubric for any AI data-platform purchase — vendors typically address one or two and leave the rest to the buyer.
insights.locator: If I would name those four pillar problems

insights.claim: In large enterprises each team builds its own AI stack with its own tool choices and its own data interfaces — one picks LangChain, another writes its own — and that fragmentation is what prevents scaling.
insights.speaker: Jörg Schad
insights.so_what: Per-team stack proliferation is the enterprise condition that creates demand for a standardised middle layer — the market opening these platforms target.
insights.locator: I've seen a lot of enterprises where basically each team

insights.claim: Current data architectures fail organisationally because data and metadata are split across platform engineers, data product owners, ingestion teams, architects, stewards, engineering, governance and consumers, each owning one slice and forced to coordinate.
insights.speaker: Jörg Schad
insights.so_what: Coordination overhead across eight-plus personas is the hidden latency in every enterprise data request, and the target any consolidation product must beat.
insights.locator: The Data 2.0 Problem

insights.claim: The technical counterpart is a data management hairball of separate tools for cataloging, governance, quality (Monte Carlo, Soda, Great Expectations), lineage and multiple ETL pipelines that each team must weave together itself.
insights.speaker: Jörg Schad
insights.so_what: Names the incumbent point-solution stack that a consolidated data-product layer would displace — the competitive set for this category.
insights.locator: If we take a look at the same problem but just from the architecture perspective

insights.claim: The proposed shape of the solution is an hourglass of standardization modelled on the LLVM compiler stack: many frontends, many backends, one standardised intermediate layer where optimisation happens.
insights.speaker: Jörg Schad
insights.so_what: The hourglass is the structural pattern that historically creates durable platform value — whoever owns the waist of the data hourglass captures the category.
insights.locator: It always reminds me of the LLVM stack

insights.claim: The explicit analogy is that data now needs what Docker and Kubernetes gave microservices — standardised containerisation of data assets plus orchestration — because infrastructure, storage, compute and security foundations already exist but are not woven together.
insights.speaker: Jörg Schad
insights.so_what: Frames the investment thesis: the data layer is pre-Kubernetes, meaning a standardisation event is still ahead rather than behind.
insights.locator: Background

insights.claim: Data complexity is multiplicative across five dimensions — storage locations and regions, access modes (RAG, MCP, vector embeddings, SQL notebooks, Power BI), processing engines (Spark, Polars, Snowflake, Iceberg lakehouse), applications, and human personas.
insights.speaker: Jörg Schad
insights.so_what: Multiplicative dimensionality is why point integrations never converge; it justifies an abstraction layer rather than more connectors.
insights.locator: Our data complexity is growing based on the number of different dimensions

insights.claim: LangChain benchmarks cited show agent performance decreasing as more context and more tools are exposed, so there is a sweet spot of information volume beyond which the model cannot decide what is relevant and hallucinates.
insights.speaker: Jörg Schad
insights.so_what: Context rot means more integration is not better — a direct argument against the 'expose the whole warehouse via one MCP endpoint' approach many vendors are shipping.
insights.locator: Context Rot: How Increasing Input Tokens Impacts LLM Performance

insights.claim: The framing for context scoping is employee onboarding: you would give a new hire the specific information they need, not the entire company handbook, and agents should be treated the same way.
insights.speaker: Jörg Schad
insights.so_what: A memorable heuristic for scoping agent context that translates directly into tool-exposure policy.
insights.quote: If we onboard someone new to our company, would we give them the entire company handbook, or would we give them specific information they need for their onboarding?
insights.locator: Context Rot: How Increasing Input Tokens Impacts LLM Performance

insights.claim: The natural but wrong default the speaker observes is exposing the entire data warehouse through a single MCP endpoint, which maximises the context-rot problem.
insights.speaker: Jörg Schad
insights.so_what: Identifies the most common enterprise MCP anti-pattern currently being deployed, and predicts a wave of remediation work.
insights.locator: We talked a little bit about this context rot

insights.claim: A data product is positioned as the equivalent of a container in the microservice world: a single asset that encapsulates data, metadata and access paths so a consumer receives one reference rather than needing to know where the data physically lives.
insights.speaker: Jörg Schad
insights.so_what: The container analogy is the conceptual unit that makes data assets composable and shareable by URL — the precondition for agent-scale consumption.
insights.quote: A data product is the equivalent to a container in the microservice world.
insights.locator: Autonomous Data Products

insights.claim: An autonomous data product is distinguished from generic 'data product' definitions by being a running process with its own runtime controller, described as a kernel, that manages its lifecycle.
insights.speaker: Jörg Schad
insights.so_what: The runtime-process definition is what separates this from cataloging products; it also implies ongoing compute cost per data product.
insights.locator: What is the idea or definition of an autonomous data product?

insights.claim: The data product lifecycle runs sense-inputs, run-transform, check-quality, then promote — and the transform layer is not replaced, since the data product encapsulates an existing Spark job or Databricks SQL transformation rather than substituting for it.
insights.speaker: Jörg Schad
insights.so_what: Non-displacement of existing compute engines lowers adoption friction and means this layer sells alongside, not against, Databricks and Snowflake.
insights.locator: Next stage of the lifecycle is in actually running the transform

insights.claim: Each data product exposes standard OpenAPI-driven endpoints for observability and discovery — inputs, outputs, current status, models, event tree and the transformation code — so users need not jump between multiple systems to understand it.
insights.speaker: Jörg Schad
insights.so_what: API-uniform metadata is what makes data assets machine-discoverable by agents, which is the functional requirement catalog tools do not meet.
insights.locator: Data product also is exposing standard APIs for observability and discovery

insights.claim: The same semantic data model is exposed through multiple output ports for different consumers — SQL for analysts, file-based for model training, vector embeddings for chatbots, and MCP for autonomous querying — separating logical from physical representation.
insights.speaker: Jörg Schad
insights.so_what: Multi-modal output from one semantic definition is the core product claim; it is also the feature that makes the layer sticky once adopted.
insights.locator: Then, last but not least, talking about the downstream consumers

insights.claim: Current data quality tooling alerts post-fact: by the time Monte Carlo, Soda or Great Expectations report that data is wrong, downstream consumers have already read it and agents may have acted on it.
insights.speaker: Jörg Schad
insights.so_what: Post-hoc quality alerting is structurally incompatible with autonomous consumption — a genuine displacement risk for the observability-style data quality vendors.
insights.locator: In this current world, what's happening is my Soda, Monte Carlo, Great Expectations

insights.claim: In the autonomous data product model, quality checks act as data contracts executed inside the lifecycle before output is promoted, with a standard interface that can still call Monte Carlo, Soda or Great Expectations.
insights.speaker: Jörg Schad
insights.so_what: Repositions incumbent quality tools as pluggable checkers inside someone else's control plane — value migrates to the orchestration layer.
insights.locator: Before we make it accessible to the downstream consumers

insights.claim: The justification for pre-consumption quality gating is that a human might notice data looks wrong but an agent is very unlikely to detect it.
insights.speaker: Jörg Schad
insights.so_what: Removing the human sanity check is the specific reason agentic pipelines require stronger upstream guarantees than analytics pipelines ever did.
insights.quote: An agent's very unlikely to detect, this data looks wrong.
insights.locator: Because we want to enable all those agents

insights.claim: Encapsulating all output modalities in one data product keeps them in lockstep, eliminating the common failure where a parallel embedding pipeline and a SQL pipeline drift days out of sync.
insights.speaker: Jörg Schad
insights.so_what: Cross-modality staleness is an under-recognised failure mode in RAG deployments; single-lifecycle updating is a concrete architectural fix.
insights.locator: Modality shift

themes.theme: Policy as contract, governance without bottleneck

insights.claim: The prevailing governance model — a governance team manually reviewing and approving each data product before release — makes that team the bottleneck and drastically slows release cycles.
insights.speaker: Jörg Schad
insights.so_what: Governance review latency is the practical brake on enterprise AI velocity, which is why automated policy enforcement is the higher-leverage investment.
insights.quote: Because the governance team typically becomes a bottleneck in reviewing those.
insights.locator: Safe Autonomous Data Consumption

insights.claim: The alternative is policies defined upfront in a central contract repository — for example, that a data product with an MCP or embedding output port must implement a predefined PII check — which every data product must satisfy to deploy on the mesh.
insights.speaker: Jörg Schad
insights.so_what: Policy-as-contract converts governance from a review queue into an invariant, which is the only model that scales to agent-speed data publication.
insights.locator: The idea behind data mesh or behind autonomous data products

insights.claim: The enforcement model is a Kubernetes admission controller analogue with one difference: policies are checked at deployment and again at runtime, so newly added policies still apply to already-deployed data products.
insights.speaker: Jörg Schad
insights.so_what: Runtime re-checking is what makes retroactive policy change possible without redeploying every asset — a requirement in regulated environments where rules change mid-flight.
insights.locator: If you want to imagine, if you're familiar with Kubernetes, Admission Controller

insights.claim: In the demo the visible global policy checks include data completeness and confirmation that email addresses and social security numbers are not exposed, shown as pass/fail status on the data product page.
insights.speaker: Jörg Schad
insights.so_what: Machine-checkable PII exposure status per data asset is the artifact a CISO needs before approving agent access at scale.
insights.locator: Last, I can also see which of those global policies are being satisfied

insights.claim: Progressive tool discovery exploits the fact that MCP's list-tools endpoint is subscribable and therefore dynamic: the gateway initially exposes only a single discover_tools call, and task-specific tools appear only after the agent states what it is trying to achieve.
insights.speaker: Jörg Schad
insights.so_what: A concrete, protocol-native mechanism for limiting context rot that any MCP server operator can implement today.
insights.locator: Agent Lifecycle with Progressive Tool Discovery

insights.claim: A single MCP gateway fronting the whole mesh centralises authorisation so each team no longer implements its own way of authorising and standardising access, and tools are re-filtered after each agent loop completes.
insights.speaker: Jörg Schad
insights.so_what: One gateway becomes both the context-control and the access-control choke point — architecturally the most valuable position in an agentic data stack.
insights.locator: The nice thing is the access is all controlled through the single gateway

insights.claim: The speaker explicitly expects MCP to require multiple further protocol iterations before it is really useful, and frames the pattern as protocol-agnostic so it applies to whatever succeeds MCP.
insights.speaker: Jörg Schad
insights.so_what: A practitioner discounting the durability of today's dominant agent protocol argues for betting on patterns rather than on protocol-specific tooling.
insights.quote: If I say MCP, I personally believe there need to be multiple iterations on that protocol to become really useful.
insights.locator: In short, basically the MCP protocol

insights.claim: Because MCP output ports are defined as part of the data product, the way MCP tools are built is standardised, letting the data product developer declare which questions their product answers best rather than having a separate team build an MCP server alongside it.
insights.speaker: Jörg Schad
insights.so_what: Co-locating tool definitions with data definitions is what prevents the sprawl of orphaned MCP servers that enterprises are already accumulating.
insights.locator: I think the first important aspect of this pattern

insights.claim: The core inversion in Data 3.0 is deciding the semantic domain model first and the physical representation second, instead of the current stack where the first decision is Snowflake or Databricks.
insights.speaker: Jörg Schad
insights.so_what: If semantics precede storage, warehouse vendors become interchangeable backends — a direct threat to the lock-in economics of the incumbent platforms.
insights.locator: Data 3.0 Autonomous Abstraction

insights.claim: Self-orchestration moves the decision of when a transformation runs from a central pipeline team to the data product owner, based on sensed input changes rather than fixed schedules.
insights.speaker: Jörg Schad
insights.so_what: Event-driven run policies replace cron-style pipelines, which is both a cost lever and a freshness lever for data platforms.
insights.locator: Orchestration shift

insights.claim: The speaker argues large Spark jobs running hourly regardless of consumption are great for Databricks revenue but waste enterprise compute when the output is accessed monthly for a CEO report.
insights.speaker: Jörg Schad
insights.so_what: Names a direct misalignment between consumption-priced data platforms and customer cost efficiency — the wedge that run-policy tooling monetises.
insights.quote: This is great for Databricks because they get a lot of money through that. It's not great for the enterprise because we often waste a lot of compute resources
insights.locator: I've seen so many Spark jobs, large-scale Spark jobs

insights.claim: Lineage comes for free inside the data product abstraction rather than requiring a separate lineage system stitched across tools, enabling decision justification down to data version and the model trained on it.
insights.speaker: Jörg Schad
insights.so_what: Built-in lineage is the audit substrate AI decision justification will require, and it removes a whole category of standalone lineage spend.
insights.locator: Then from the reasoning shift

insights.claim: The infrastructure team's role shrinks to providing self-serve infrastructure profiles that abstract compute such as a Spark instance, removing them as the first point of contact for data access requests and debugging.
insights.speaker: Jörg Schad
insights.so_what: The organisational payoff is removing infrastructure teams from the data-request critical path, which is where most enterprise data latency actually accrues.
insights.locator: With the data products, they only need to provide a self-serve infrastructure

insights.claim: The worked example pairs two input data products of different modality and cadence — minute-level structured Amazon-style reviews and weekly scanned PDF point-of-sale feedback — to show that the update policy is a per-product configuration decision rather than a platform default.
insights.speaker: Jörg Schad
insights.so_what: Mixed-cadence multimodal inputs are the normal enterprise case, and the freshness decision is where compute cost is actually set.
insights.locator: Example

insights.claim: In the demo, a single data product exposes output ports on Snowflake, Iceberg on S3 and vector embeddings in Pinecone, with a trust summary showing access frequency and how often it passes its own checks, plus a pluggable access-request flow that can raise a Jira ticket or run automatically.
insights.speaker: Jörg Schad
insights.so_what: Trust metrics attached to each asset — usage plus check pass rate — are the discovery signal agents and humans need to choose between competing datasets.
insights.locator: In this case, I have it on Snowflake, I have it on Iceberg NS3

insights.claim: The closing argument is that the specific implementation matters less than the principle: domain-centric GenAI use cases that avoid exposing too much information are what make a data architecture both scalable and safe.
insights.speaker: Jörg Schad
insights.so_what: The durable takeaway is a design constraint rather than a product, which is how architectural patterns spread ahead of the vendors that popularise them.
insights.quote: keeping in mind domain-centric GenAI and domain-centric use cases, not exposing too much information, it actually really helps you to build a scalable and safe data architecture.
insights.locator: Key Insight
